questions.prompt: What makes a container lighter than a virtual machine?
options: It shares the host kernel instead of running its own
questions.explanation: Containers are isolated processes on the host kernel, so there is no second operating system to boot.

questions.prompt: What do Linux namespaces provide to a container?
options: Isolation of things like processes, network and filesystem
questions.explanation: Namespaces are what make a container see its own limited view of the system.

questions.prompt: What do cgroups control?
options: Resource limits such as CPU and memory
questions.explanation: Control groups cap how much of a resource a container is allowed to consume.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an image and a container?
options: An image is the template, a container is a running instance of it
An image runs, a container is stored
questions.explanation: You build or pull an image, then run containers from it, and many containers can come from one image.

questions.prompt: What happens to files written inside a container when it is removed?
options: They are lost unless stored in a volume
questions.explanation: The writable layer disappears with the container, which is why volumes exist.

questions.prompt: Which command gets you a shell inside an already running container?
questions.explanation: exec starts a new process inside the existing container without restarting it.

questions.prompt: What does docker ps -a show that docker ps does not?
questions.explanation: Without -a you only see running containers, so stopped ones look invisible.

questions.prompt: Why is depending on the latest tag risky?
options: It can change underneath you without warning
questions.explanation: The same tag can point at different content over time, so builds stop being reproducible.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a bind mount and a named volume?
options: A bind mount maps a host path, a named volume is managed by Docker
questions.explanation: Bind mounts point at a specific host directory, while named volumes are stored and managed by Docker.

questions.prompt: How do two containers on a custom network reach each other?
questions.explanation: Docker provides name resolution on user defined networks, so service names work as hostnames.

questions.prompt: Why should a container log to stdout rather than a file inside itself?
options: So the logs can be collected by the platform and survive the container
questions.explanation: Logs written inside the container die with it, while stdout can be shipped somewhere durable.

questions.prompt: What does docker system prune do?
options: Removes unused containers, networks and images to reclaim space
questions.explanation: It cleans up unused objects, which matters because Docker fills disks quietly.

questions.prompt: A container is just a process running on the host with restricted visibility.
questions.explanation: You can see it in the host process list, which is why containers start so much faster than virtual machines.

questions.prompt: Two containers can be published to the same host port at the same time.
questions.explanation: The second one fails to bind, exactly as two services on one port would on a normal Linux machine.

questions.prompt: Data in a named volume survives removing and recreating the container.
questions.explanation: That separation between the container lifecycle and the data is the whole reason volumes exist.

questions.prompt: What does the FROM instruction do in a Dockerfile?
options: Sets the base image to build on
questions.explanation: Every image starts from a base, and FROM names it.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
options: ENTRYPOINT sets the fixed command, CMD provides default arguments that can be overridden
questions.explanation: ENTRYPOINT defines what always runs, and CMD supplies defaults that a run command can replace.

questions.prompt: Why should you copy dependency files before copying your source code?
options: So the dependency install layer stays cached when only code changes
questions.explanation: Docker caches layers in order, so putting the slow step above the fast changing step saves rebuild time.

questions.prompt: What invalidates a Docker layer cache?
options: A change to that instruction or to the files it copies
questions.explanation: Once a layer changes, every layer after it must be rebuilt too.

questions.prompt: What does a dockerignore file do?
options: Keeps files out of the build context sent to Docker
questions.explanation: A smaller build context means faster builds and fewer accidental inclusions.

questions.prompt: What is the point of a multi stage build?
options: Building in one stage and shipping only the artifact in the final image
questions.explanation: Build tools stay in the earlier stage, so the final image carries only what it needs to run.

questions.prompt: Why do smaller images matter?
options: Faster pulls, less storage cost and a smaller attack surface
questions.explanation: Size affects deployment speed, storage bills and how much software could contain a vulnerability.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of a container running as root by default?
options: A container escape or flaw has far more power on the host
questions.explanation: Running unprivileged limits what a compromise inside the container can reach.

questions.prompt: Why is putting a secret in a Dockerfile dangerous?
options: It stays visible in the image history to anyone who pulls it
questions.explanation: Layers are inspectable, so a secret in a build instruction is effectively published with the image.

questions.prompt: Why pin a base image to a specific version?
options: So builds stay reproducible instead of changing when the tag moves
questions.explanation: Pinning means today's build and next month's build produce the same thing.

questions.prompt: What is ECR?
options: A private container registry in AWS
questions.explanation: ECR stores your images inside your AWS account rather than on a public registry.

questions.prompt: What is the safest way for an EC2 instance to pull from ECR?
options: Store access keys on the instance
questions.explanation: The instance role supplies temporary credentials with no long lived secret on disk.

questions.prompt: Combining several RUN commands into one reduces the number of image layers.
questions.explanation: Each RUN creates a layer, so merging them produces a smaller and simpler image.

questions.prompt: Deleting a secret in a later Docker layer removes it from the image.
questions.explanation: Earlier layers still contain it, so the only fix is rebuilding without the secret ever being added.

questions.prompt: An ECR lifecycle policy can automatically delete old images to control storage cost.
questions.explanation: Without one, every build you ever pushed keeps costing money.

questions.prompt: What problem does Docker Compose solve?
options: Defining and running multi container applications from one file
questions.explanation: Compose replaces long run commands with a declarative file describing all the services.

questions.prompt: How does one compose service reach another?
options: By using the service name as a hostname
questions.explanation: Compose puts services on a shared network with name resolution between them.

questions.prompt: What does depends_on actually guarantee?
options: Only the start order, not readiness
questions.explanation: Start order is not readiness, which is why healthchecks are needed for databases.

questions.prompt: Why add a healthcheck to a database service?
options: So dependent services wait until it can actually accept connections
questions.explanation: A started container is not necessarily an available one, and healthchecks close that gap.

questions.prompt: Why should configuration come from environment variables rather than the image?
options: So one image can run in different environments without rebuilding
questions.explanation: The same artifact should move from staging to production with only its configuration changing.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a gitignore for this kind of project?
options: Env files, keys and local state
questions.explanation: Anything secret or machine specific should never reach the repository.

questions.prompt: Where would a production system store database credentials?
options: In a secrets manager or parameter store
questions.explanation: Dedicated secret storage keeps credentials out of code and out of images.

questions.prompt: What does a restart policy do?
options: Brings the container back automatically after a crash or reboot
questions.explanation: Without one, a rebooted host comes back with nothing running.

questions.prompt: A container exits immediately. Where do you look first?
options: The container logs and the exit code
questions.explanation: The logs almost always contain the reason, and the exit code narrows the category.

questions.prompt: It works on your machine but fails in a clean environment. What is the usual cause?
options: Something on your machine that is not in the image or config
questions.explanation: Hidden local dependencies are the classic cause, and it is why reproducible builds matter.

questions.prompt: What happens when a container exceeds its memory limit?
questions.explanation: The kernel terminates the process, which usually shows up as an abrupt container exit.

questions.prompt: Which log driver sends container logs to AWS CloudWatch?
questions.explanation: The awslogs driver ships stdout straight into a CloudWatch log group.

questions.prompt: A container that starts successfully is guaranteed to be ready to serve traffic.
questions.explanation: Applications often need time to initialise, which is what readiness checks are for.

questions.prompt: Running docker compose down removes containers but a named volume can keep the data.
questions.explanation: Volumes are separate from containers, so data survives unless you explicitly remove them.

questions.prompt: You can use the networking tools from Month 2 inside a running container to debug it.
questions.explanation: A container is a normal Linux environment, so the same troubleshooting approach applies.

questions.prompt: What does git revert do that git reset does not?
options: Creates a new commit that undoes a change, leaving history intact
questions.explanation: Revert is the safe option on shared branches because it adds rather than rewrites.

questions.prompt: What causes a merge conflict?
options: Two branches changing the same lines differently
questions.explanation: Git cannot decide which version wins, so it asks you to resolve it.

questions.prompt: Why turn on branch protection for main?
options: So changes go through review and checks instead of direct pushes
questions.explanation: Protection is what makes the pipeline a real gate rather than a suggestion.

questions.prompt: In GitHub Actions, what is the relationship between a workflow, a job and a step?
options: A workflow contains jobs, and a job contains steps
questions.explanation: Workflows hold jobs, jobs run on a runner, and each job is a list of steps.

questions.prompt: What does the checkout action do?
options: Makes the repository contents available to the job
questions.explanation: Runners start empty, so the code has to be fetched before anything can use it.

questions.prompt: What is the point of running tests on every pull request?
options: To catch broken changes before they reach main
questions.explanation: The gate is only useful if it runs before the merge, not after.

questions.prompt: Why cache dependencies in a workflow?
options: To make runs faster by avoiding repeated downloads
questions.explanation: Caching cuts the slowest repeated step out of most runs.

questions.prompt: How should a workflow get access to AWS?
questions.explanation: Secrets or short lived OIDC credentials keep long lived keys out of the repository.

questions.prompt: GitHub masks secrets in logs. Why is that not full protection?
options: A step can still write the value somewhere else or transform it
questions.explanation: Masking hides exact matches, but a determined or careless step can still leak the value.

questions.prompt: Why tag an image with the commit SHA?
options: So every deployed image traces back to exact source code
questions.explanation: Traceability from a running container back to a commit is essential when something breaks.

questions.prompt: What should happen to a pull request when a required check fails?
questions.explanation: A gate that can be ignored is not a gate.

questions.prompt: Why add a timeout to a CI job?
options: So a hung job cannot run indefinitely and consume minutes
questions.explanation: Without a timeout, one stuck job can burn resources until someone notices.

questions.prompt: A failing test that blocks a deploy is the pipeline working correctly.
questions.explanation: Stopping a broken change before it ships is exactly what the pipeline is for.

questions.prompt: Committing a secret and then deleting it in the next commit removes it from the repository.
questions.explanation: It stays in the history, so the credential must be treated as compromised and rotated.

questions.prompt: Scoping CI permissions to only what the deploy needs reduces the damage of a leaked credential.
questions.explanation: Least privilege applies to automation exactly as it applies to people.

questions.prompt: What is the goal of a continuous deployment pipeline?
options: Code reaching the target environment with no manual steps
questions.explanation: The pipeline replaces the manual sequence a person would otherwise perform by hand every time.

questions.prompt: Why deploy to staging before production?
options: To catch problems in a safe environment first
questions.explanation: Staging is where a bad change costs nothing, which is the point of having it.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest reliable rollback method?
options: Redeploy the previous known good image tag
questions.explanation: Because images are immutable and tagged, the last good one is still there and ready to run.

questions.prompt: Why does immutable tagging make rollback easy?
options: The exact previous artifact still exists and can be redeployed
questions.explanation: Nothing needs rebuilding, so recovery is a pull and a restart.

questions.prompt: Why run two containers behind a proxy during deployment?
options: So one can serve traffic while the other is replaced
questions.explanation: Replacing them one at a time is what removes the gap in service.

questions.prompt: What should gate traffic to a newly deployed container?
questions.explanation: Sending traffic before the app is ready produces errors that look like a failed deploy.

questions.prompt: How would you measure deployment downtime?
options: Send requests in a loop during the deploy and count failures
questions.explanation: Measuring it directly turns downtime from a feeling into a number you can improve.

questions.prompt: Why does a failed deploy need a notification?
options: So you find out without having to check manually
questions.explanation: An unnoticed failure means production silently stays on the old version, or worse.

questions.prompt: Which statement is strongest on a CV?
options: Built a pipeline that cut deployment time from 20 minutes to under 2
questions.explanation: A measured outcome shows what you did, while a tool list only shows what you have touched.

questions.prompt: The pipeline succeeds but the site serves old code. What do you check?
options: Whether the deploy step pulled the new tag and restarted the container
questions.explanation: A green build only proves the image was made, not that the running container was replaced.

questions.prompt: Why should the deploy use a specific tag rather than latest?
options: So you know exactly which build is running
questions.explanation: With latest you cannot tell what is deployed, which makes both debugging and rollback guesswork.

questions.prompt: What makes a project repository valuable to an employer?
options: A clear README, a working pipeline and a documented architecture
questions.explanation: Reviewers look for evidence of thinking and operation, not volume of code.

questions.prompt: A build that works locally but fails in CI usually means something on your machine is not captured in the repository.
questions.explanation: That gap is the exact problem containers and pipelines exist to eliminate.

questions.prompt: Manual approval before a production deploy defeats the purpose of automation.
questions.explanation: Automating the work while keeping a human decision point is a normal and sensible pattern.

questions.prompt: Being able to change one line, push it, and watch it reach production is a reasonable end goal for this month.
questions.explanation: That single demonstration covers containers, registries, CI, deployment and rollback in one story.
